---
title: "Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/common.R")
cal <- readRDS("data/calibration.rds")
rel <- cal$reliability
met <- cal$metrics
raw <- met[met$method == "Raw VendorScore", ]
iso <- met[met$method == "Isotonic-calibrated", ]
top <- rel[rel$score == "Raw VendorScore" & rel$bin == 10, ]
raw_rel <- rel[rel$score == "Raw VendorScore", ]
n_under <- sum(raw_rel$observed > raw_rel$predicted)
mv <- cal$vendor_tiers
ci <- cal$boot_ci
```

## The question

When VendorScore says a vendor has a 10% chance of an incident, do incidents happen about
10% of the time? RiskMetric Systems asserts that its scores are "well-calibrated." NorthPoint
cannot inspect the model, but it can compare the scores with what happened. Here we test
the claim on months 31 to 48, which the vendor never saw.

## Method in brief

We sort the `r format(300 * 18, big.mark = ",")` evaluation-window vendor-months
into ten equal-sized groups by score, then compare each group's average score with its
observed incident rate. That comparison is a *reliability diagram*. We summarise it with
the Brier score (average squared error of the probabilities; lower is better) and the
expected calibration error, ECE (the average gap between score and outcome across groups).
A kernel calibration test asks whether the gaps are larger than chance would produce.

To repair the scores without touching the vendor's code, we fit an isotonic regression (a
monotone step-function mapping) that converts raw scores into calibrated ones. It is fit on
months 1 to 30 only, so every number below comes from months 31 to 48, which the
calibrator never saw. Platt scaling, a smoother alternative, is in the table. Both come
from the `probcal` package.

## Findings

```{r}
#| label: fig-reliability
#| fig-cap: "Reliability diagram, months 31–48. Points are score deciles with 95% intervals; dashed line is the true average incident rate."
#| fig-alt: "Predicted versus observed incident rate on log axes for raw and isotonic-calibrated scores, with a diagonal and a horizontal reference line."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
ggplot(rel, aes(predicted, observed, colour = score, shape = score)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = cal$base_rate_true, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), width = 0.04, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(okabe_ito[c("vermillion", "blue")])) +
  labs(x = "Average predicted probability (log scale)",
       y = "Observed incident rate (log scale)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL)
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Each dot groups vendor-months with similar scores. Left to right
is what the model predicted; bottom to top is what actually happened. A dot on the grey
diagonal means the model was right on average. The lines through each dot show the range
of plausible outcomes, given that incidents are rare.

**What the plot tells you.** The highest-scored group sits below the diagonal: the model
said about `r pct(top$predicted)`, and `r pct(top$observed)` of those vendor-months had an
incident. Most lower-scored groups sit above the diagonal, so the model understated their
risk. With only about 100 incidents, the intervals are wide. The pattern is
suggestive but not conclusive for any single group.
:::

The raw scores are overconfident at both ends. The top-scored group was told it faced a
`r pct(top$predicted)` risk, but its observed rate was `r pct(top$observed)`, with an interval
(`r pct(top$low)` to `r pct(top$high)`) that excludes the prediction. In `r n_under` of 10 groups the observed rate exceeded
the score, mostly the low-scored ones. The kernel test rejects "well-calibrated"
(p = `r pval(cal$claim_test$p.value)`), though with this few incidents we read that as
moderate evidence, not proof.

At the portfolio level the picture is kinder: raw scores imply `r num(raw$expected_per_month, 1)`
incidents a month, against `r num(cal$observed_per_month, 1)` observed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration metrics, months 31–48. Lower Brier and ECE are better; the last column compares with observed incidents per month."
tab <- met[, c("method", "brier", "ece_mass", "ece_width", "expected_per_month")]
tab <- rbind(tab, data.frame(method = "Observed", brier = NA, ece_mass = NA,
                             ece_width = NA, expected_per_month = cal$observed_per_month))
knitr::kable(tab, digits = c(0, 4, 4, 4, 1), na = "—",
             col.names = c("Scores", "Brier", "ECE (equal-size groups)",
                           "ECE (equal-width groups)", "Incidents per month"))
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** Each row is a version of the scores: the vendor's raw output,
two adjusted versions, and the actual count. Smaller Brier and ECE numbers mean more honest
probabilities. ECE is shown with two common ways of grouping scores, because the choice
matters. The last column is the number of incidents the scores imply each month.

**What the table tells you.** Isotonic adjustment lowers the Brier score slightly and
lowers ECE with equal-size groups, but raises it with equal-width groups, so the two ECE
versions disagree. Re-sampling vendors, the Brier change is `r num(1e4 * ci["50%", "d_brier"], 1)`
in units of 0.0001, with an interval of `r num(1e4 * ci["2.5%", "d_brier"], 1)` to `r num(1e4 * ci["97.5%", "d_brier"], 1)`:
close to zero. The adjusted scores also imply only `r num(iso$expected_per_month, 1)` incidents a month,
well below the `r num(cal$observed_per_month, 1)` observed.
:::

Recalibration helps less than hoped. The improvement in Brier score is small, its interval
reaches zero, and ECE moves in opposite directions depending on how groups are formed.
Worse, the adjusted scores undercount incidents by about
`r pct(1 - iso$expected_per_month / cal$observed_per_month, 0)`. The calibrator learned the
months 1 to 30 base rate, but incidents rose afterwards (Page 3), so a mapping fit on
older data goes stale.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tiers
#| fig-cap: "Vendors by risk tier under raw versus calibrated scores (Low <1%, Medium 1–3%, High >3% monthly probability; illustrative thresholds)."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart counting vendors that keep or change risk tier after isotonic calibration."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
mov <- cal$moves
mov$path <- factor(paste(mov$from, "→", mov$to),
                   levels = unique(paste(mov$from, "→", mov$to)[order(mov$move != "No change", mov$from)]))
ggplot(mov, aes(path, Freq, fill = move)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No change" = unname(okabe_ito["grey"]),
                               "Moves down" = unname(okabe_ito["blue"]),
                               "Moves up" = unname(okabe_ito["vermillion"]))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "Tier under raw → calibrated scores", y = "Number of vendors", fill = NULL)
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Vendors are placed in Low, Medium or High risk tiers using their
average score over months 31 to 48. Each bar counts vendors by their tier before and after
adjustment, for example "Medium → Low". Blue bars are vendors moving to a lower tier.

**What the plot tells you.** Most vendors, `r sum(mv$move == "No change")` of 300, stay
where they are. All `r sum(mv$move != "No change")` that move go down, none up. The model's
excess confidence mostly inflated vendors at the top of its ranking. The tier thresholds
are illustrative, so the exact counts would shift with other cut-offs.
:::

## So what

The vendor's calibration claim does not hold cleanly for NorthPoint's own outcomes. The
largest overstatement sits where decisions matter most, with the highest-risk vendors, which
the guidance's outcomes analysis (§V) is meant to catch. Recalibration is a legitimate
overlay (§VII) because the bank adjusts the output and leaves the vendor's code alone. But
it is not a one-off fix: it needs refreshing as conditions move, and it inherits the
limits of the data used to fit it.

This is partial validation. It shows that the scores are miscalibrated; it cannot say why,
and it cannot tell us whether the proprietary method is conceptually sound.

## Committee action

Sound practice suggests including a reliability diagram in every validation pack, and
setting explicit calibration thresholds that trigger recalibration, with a scheduled
refit of any overlay. The April 2026 interagency *Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk
Management* leaves the thresholds to the bank's judgement.
